# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction
Symptomatic heart failure (HF) continues to present a major global health challenge despite significant advances in pharmacological therapies [1, 2]. While guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and device-based interventions such as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) have revolutionized the care of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), a substantial proportion of symptomatic patients remain ineligible for CRT because of a narrow QRS complex (<120 ms) [1-3]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as an innovative bioelectronic therapy to address this therapeutic gap, delivering non-excitatory electrical impulses during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle to enhance myocardial function without increasing oxygen consumption [3-5].

## Mechanisms of Action
The foundational work on the clinical application of CCM began with seminal human experiences showing acute hemodynamic improvements [6, 7]. The therapy delivers high-voltage, biphasic electrical signals during the absolute refractory period of the ventricular action potential, meaning they do not trigger a new contraction but instead modulate ongoing cellular processes [4, 5]. At the molecular level, failing cardiomyocytes exhibit aberrant calcium handling, which is characterized by the downregulation of sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase 2a (SERCA2a) and the hypophosphorylation of phospholamban [5]. 

CCM reverses these pathological mechanisms. Acutely, it enhances calcium influx through L-type calcium channels and restores intracellular calcium handling, facilitating a localized increase in contractility [5-7]. Chronically, animal and clinical studies have demonstrated that repeated CCM delivery reverses the maladaptive fetal gene expression program, restores cytoskeletal proteins, and upregulates calcium-handling proteins [4, 5, 8]. Importantly, these benefits propagate beyond the lead implantation site, driving global left ventricular reverse remodeling, improving myocardial efficiency, and altering autonomic tone to dampen sympathetic hyperactivity [6, 8].

## Evolution of Clinical Trials
The clinical efficacy and safety of CCM have been established across several key randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The first double-blind, randomized crossover trial, FIX-HF-4, showed that CCM significantly improves peak oxygen consumption (peak $\text{VO}_2$) and quality of life [9]. This was followed by the larger FIX-HF-5 trial, which enrolled 428 patients with New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III/IV heart failure and LVEF $\le$35% [10]. Although the primary endpoint of ventilatory anaerobic threshold was not met in the overall cohort, a prespecified subgroup analysis showed highly significant improvements in patients with moderately reduced LVEF (25% to 45%) [11].

To prospectively confirm these findings in the target population, the FIX-HF-5C confirmatory trial randomized 160 patients with NYHA class III/IV symptoms, LVEF 25%–45%, and a narrow QRS complex to CCM plus medical therapy versus medical therapy alone [12]. The FIX-HF-5C trial met its primary safety and efficacy endpoints, showing significant improvements in peak $\text{VO}_2$, 6-minute hall walk distance, and quality of life, alongside a reduction in the composite of cardiovascular death and HF hospitalizations [12]. Furthermore, the subsequent FIX-HF-5C2 trial demonstrated that a simplified two-lead Optimizer system (eliminating the atrial sensing lead) provides equivalent safety, efficacy, and signal delivery while reducing procedural complexity and lead complications [13].

## Real-World and Long-Term Evidence
Long-term observational datasets and real-world registries have confirmed the translation of clinical trial efficacy into real-world practice. The European Optimizer Smart registry study (CCM-REG) tracked patients for up to 3 years, revealing sustained improvements in functional class and LVEF, as well as a significant survival benefit [14]. Long-term cohort studies have similarly demonstrated that CCM therapy reduces the composite of cardiovascular mortality and heart failure-related hospitalizations over extended follow-up [15]. While early trials focused heavily on HFrEF, the potential benefits of CCM are also being explored in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). The pilot CCM-HFpEF study demonstrated that CCM is safe and significantly improves patient-reported health status and quality of life in symptomatic HFpEF patients (LVEF $\ge$50%) [16].

## Efficacy, Quality of Life, and Patient Selection
Comprehensive meta-analyses have reinforced the therapeutic impact of CCM. A robust individual patient data meta-analysis confirmed that CCM significantly improves objective exercise capacity and subjective quality of life, as measured by the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire [17]. These benefits help fill a critical gap in contemporary heart failure care [18, 19]. Earlier meta-analyses had similarly highlighted consistent functional improvements [20], while long-term single-center cohorts confirmed that CCM is not associated with increased arrhythmic burden [21]. Importantly, long-term delivery of CCM signals has not been associated with widening of the QRS interval, indicating that it does not induce ventricular dyssynchrony [22].

Furthermore, observational data from registries have shed light on the efficacy of CCM in broader patient subgroups. Patients with mild symptoms (NYHA class II) can also derive significant clinical benefits from CCM, suggesting a potential role for earlier intervention [23]. Another study indicated that functional improvements and reverse remodeling are achieved regardless of the underlying heart failure etiology, showing comparable efficacy in both ischemic and non-ischemic cardiomyopathy [24]. This is particularly promising given that a large proportion of the heart failure population is symptomatic despite GDMT and ineligible for CRT, thus representing potential candidates for CCM [25].

## Guidelines and Future Horizons
Given this robust body of evidence, current guidelines now recognize CCM with a class IIb recommendation for symptomatic HFrEF or HFmrEF patients with narrow QRS complexes [1, 2, 26, 27]. Chronic CCM stimulation has also been shown to improve left ventricular global longitudinal strain and myocardial mechano-energetic efficiency in this cohort [28]. As next-generation device configurations emerge, they aim to further streamline therapy delivery and broaden patient access [29]. Finally, the clinical integration of CCM with existing implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) systems or subcutaneous ICDs (S-ICDs) has been shown to be feasible, safe, and free from electromagnetic interference, allowing for the simultaneous management of contractility dysfunction and sudden cardiac death risk [30].

## Conclusion
CCM represents a major milestone in device-based HF therapy. By directly addressing the calcium handling and gene transcription abnormalities that characterize the failing myocardium, it provides inotropic support without increasing myocardial oxygen consumption. For symptomatic HF patients with a narrow QRS complex who are on optimal medical therapy but remain limited by their disease, CCM offers a safe, effective, and guideline-supported strategy to improve functional capacity, enhance quality of life, and reduce hospitalizations.
